summary: A robot is a chain of frames, each placed relative to the one before. You pack a rotation and a translation into one 4 × 4 matrix, derive its inverse without a general matrix inversion, and locate a point seen by a wrist camera in the robot’s base frame.
html:
Rotation plus translation in one matrix

A rigid-body pose is a rotation R and a position p. A point with coordinates xB​ in frame B has coordinates in frame A

xA​=RAB​xB​+pAB​.

This is affine, not linear, so it can’t be a 3 × 3 matrix. Append a 1 to every point, x~=(x,1), and it becomes a single matrix product:

(xA​1​)=TAB​(RAB​0⊤​pAB​1​)​​(xB​1​).

These matrices form the group SE(3). Chaining frames is multiplication, TAC​=TAB​TBC​, and the subscripts cancel like units, which is a good habit for catching mistakes. Directions (velocities, normals) get a 0 instead of a 1 so the translation doesn’t touch them.

The inverse costs almost nothing

Solve xA​=RxB​+p for xB​: xB​=R⊤xA​−R⊤p. So

T−1=(R⊤0⊤​−R⊤p1​).

No general 4 × 4 inversion, no pivoting, and the result stays exactly in SE(3). Production code should never call a generic inv on a transform.

Worked example: a wrist camera sees a bolt

The gripper frame G sits at p=(0.5,0,0.3) m in the base frame B, rotated 90° about z. A camera on the gripper reports a bolt at xG​=(0.1,0,0) m.

  1. Rz​(90°)(0.1,0,0)=(0,0.1,0).
  2. Add the translation: xB​=(0.5,0.1,0.3) m.

The inverse transform maps the base frame into the gripper frame:

−R⊤p=−Rz​(−90°)(0.5,0,0.3)=−(0,−0.5,0.3)=(0,0.5,−0.3).

Check: T−1 applied to (0.5,0.1,0.3) gives R⊤(0.5,0.1,0.3)+(0,0.5,−0.3)=(0.1,−0.5,0.3)+(0,0.5,−0.3)=(0.1,0,0), the bolt in the camera’s frame again.

Code it from scratch

se3.py
import math
import numpy as np

def rotz(t): c, s = math.cos(t), math.sin(t); return np.array([[c, -s, 0], [s, c, 0], [0, 0, 1.0]])
def rotx(t): c, s = math.cos(t), math.sin(t); return np.array([[1.0, 0, 0], [0, c, -s], [0, s, c]])

def transform(R, p):
    T = np.eye(4); T[:3, :3] = R; T[:3, 3] = p
    return T

def inv(T):
    R, p = T[:3, :3], T[:3, 3]
    return transform(R.T, -R.T @ p)

def apply(T, x, point=True):
    return T[:3, :3] @ np.asarray(x, float) + (T[:3, 3] if point else 0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    T_BG = transform(rotz(math.pi / 2), [0.5, 0, 0.3])
    assert np.allclose(apply(T_BG, [0.1, 0, 0]), [0.5, 0.1, 0.3])
    assert np.allclose(inv(T_BG)[:3, 3], [0, 0.5, -0.3])
    assert np.allclose(apply(inv(T_BG), [0.5, 0.1, 0.3]), [0.1, 0, 0])
    assert np.allclose(apply(T_BG, [1, 0, 0], point=False), [0, 1, 0])   # directions ignore p
    rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
    for _ in range(1000):
        T = transform(rotz(rng.uniform(-3, 3)) @ rotx(rng.uniform(-3, 3)), rng.standard_normal(3))
        U = transform(rotx(rng.uniform(-3, 3)), rng.standard_normal(3))
        x = rng.standard_normal(3)
        assert np.allclose(T @ inv(T), np.eye(4), atol=1e-12)
        assert np.allclose(apply(T, x), T[:3, :3] @ x + T[:3, 3])
        assert np.allclose(apply(T @ U, x), apply(T, apply(U, x)))
    print("T @ inv(T) = I; chained transforms equal sequential application")

Exercises

A lidar is mounted 0.2 m forward and 0.4 m above a robot’s base, with no rotation. It sees an obstacle at (3,−1,−0.4) m in its own frame. Where is the obstacle in the base frame?

Show the solution

With R=I: xB​=(3,−1,−0.4)+(0.2,0,0.4)=(3.2,−1,0) m, on the ground in front and to the right.

If TWA​ places robot A in the world and TWB​ places robot B, what transform gives B’s pose as seen by A?

Show the solution

TAB​=TAW​TWB​=TWA−1​TWB​. The inner subscripts cancel: A to W to B.

quiz.q: In the worked example, what is the y coordinate of the bolt in the base frame (in metres)?
quiz.explain: Rz​(90°) turns (0.1,0,0) into (0,0.1,0); adding p gives (0.5,0.1,0.3).

quiz.q: What is the translation part of T−1?
quiz.explain: From xB​=R⊤(xA​−p).

quiz.q: To transform a velocity vector with a 4 × 4 transform, you append…
quiz.explain: Directions don’t depend on where the origin is, so the fourth coordinate is 0.

quiz.q: In the lidar example, what is the base-frame x coordinate of the obstacle?
quiz.explain: There is no rotation, so add the mounting offset, 3+0.2=3.2 m.
